<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is not a dynamic web app or microservice suite but a static content site (“Awesome Raspberry Pi”) – a curated list of links and resources.  
   - It uses a static-site generator (MkDocs), some Ruby tooling (all-contributors), Node.js for ancillary scripts, and is deployed to Netlify.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level config files  
     • mkdocs.yml – MkDocs site configuration (theme, pages, plugins)  
     • netlify.toml – Netlify build & deploy settings  
     • .github/workflows/ci.yaml – GitHub Actions definitions (lint, tests)  
     • Makefile, scripts/build.sh – local build shortcuts  
   - Language/tooling stacks  
     • requirements.txt – Python dependencies (mkdocs and plugins)  
     • Gemfile – Ruby gems (all-contributors, markdown linters)  
     • package.json – Node.js scripts or lint tooling  
     • .tool-versions – asdf definitions to pin Python, Ruby, Node versions  
   - No “src” folder – the content is Markdown in the root (README.md) and subfolders (media/…)  

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - Describes site content only (OS images, Tools, Projects, Resources) – no existing architecture diagram.  
   - Contribution guidelines trigger the all-contributors bot to update CONTRIBUTORS.md.  

4. How to create the system design diagram  
   a. Main components  
     1) Developer Workstation – clones repo, installs Python, Ruby, Node via asdf, runs “make serve” or scripts/build.sh to preview.  
     2) GitHub Repository – stores content and config, hosts PRs & Issues.  
     3) all-contributors Bot – GitHub App that updates CONTRIBUTORS.md on approved PRs.  
     4) CI Pipeline (GitHub Actions) – on PR or push, runs linters, markdown checks, build smoke tests.  
     5) Static Site Generator – MkDocs (Python process) + any Ruby/Node scripts to generate final HTML/CSS/JS.  
     6) Hosting & CDN – Netlify picks up pushes (via webhook), runs `mkdocs build`, and deploys to a global CDN.  
     7) End Users – browse the static site over HTTPS.  

   b. Relationships and interactions  
     • Developer → push to GitHub →  
       → GitHub Actions CI: lint → build → report status  
       → all-contributors Bot: on merged PR, updates CONTRIBUTORS.md  
     • Merge to main → Netlify webhook → Netlify build (mkdocs + plugins + media) → deploy → CDN  
     • User browsers fetch HTML/CSS/JS from CDN → render pages  

   c. Architectural patterns and design principles  
     • GitOps / Infrastructure-as-Code: netlify.toml + mkdocs.yml define build & deploy steps as code  
     • Immutable artifacts: every build outputs a versioned static site  
     • Separation of concerns:  
       – Content (Markdown)  
       – Build (Python/Ruby/Node toolchains)  
       – CI checks (lint/test)  
       – Deployment (Netlify)  

   d. Key technologies and frameworks  
     • GitHub Actions for CI  
     • MkDocs (Python) + MkDocs plugins  
     • Ruby all-contributors CLI  
     • Node.js scripts (if any tooling under package.json)  
     • Netlify for build and hosting  
     • asdf for version management  

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram  
   - Emphasize the pipeline flow: Developer → GitHub → CI → Netlify → CDN → Users  
   - Show language/toolchain enclaves: Python (MkDocs), Ruby (contributors), Node (scripts)  
   - Highlight automated bots (all-contributors) and infrastructure definitions (mkdocs.yml, netlify.toml)  
   - For a static site, focus on build stages and hosting – no backend or database components  

6. Elements to include in the diagram  
   - Clear component boxes: Developer, GitHub Repo, CI Server, Static Site Generator, Netlify/CDN, Users  
   - Directional arrows: commits → CI, merges → Netlify build, deployment → CDN, user requests → CDN  
   - Color-coding or distinct shapes:  
     • Code components (repo, config) in one color  
     • Build processes (CI, mkdocs, scripts) in another  
     • Hosting/CDN in a third  
   - Annotations for config files: mkdocs.yml, netlify.toml, ci.yaml  

NOTE: Keep the diagram detailed enough to capture each stage – from code commit through automated checks, site generation, and final deployment – but avoid extraneous boxes for components that don’t exist (e.g., no database or microservices).  
</explanation>
